title: Solve it: keep only the even numbers
idea: GUIDED PROBLEM (filter). A keep-only problem whose test is a remainder check (number % 2 == 0). Reinforces that any True/False test can drive a filter, and reviews % from earlier units.
problem: You have these house numbers: [11, 4, 7, 10, 2]. Build a list of only the even ones.

exercises.prompt:
PROBLEM: numbers are [11, 4, 7, 10, 2]. Build a list of only the even ones.

OUTPUT?
options: A new list of only the even numbers
exercises.explanation: 'Only the even ones' means keep matching items, so the output is a new, filtered list of the even numbers.

exercises.prompt: Example. By hand, keep the even numbers from [11, 4, 7, 10, 2]. Which stay?
exercises.explanation: Even means divisible by 2: 4, 10, and 2 qualify; 11 and 7 are odd. Kept list is [4, 10, 2] — your check value.

exercises.prompt: Plan. How do you test whether a number is even? (recall % from earlier)
exercises.explanation: % gives the remainder. An even number divided by 2 leaves remainder 0, so the test is number % 2 == 0.

exercises.prompt: Put the filter plan in order.
blocks: For each number, if it is even, add it to the evens list
exercises.explanation: Same filter recipe — only the test changed. Start empty, keep the matches, show the result.

exercises.prompt: The filter recipe (empty list, loop, if-test, append) stays the same no matter what the test is — only the condition inside the if changes.
exercises.explanation: That is the big idea of this unit: one shape, many tests. Swap '>= 50' for '% 2 == 0' and you filter evens instead of passes.

exercises.prompt: Code it. Arrange the lines (empty list, loop + test + append, show).
exercises.explanation: Store the numbers, start evens empty, keep each number with remainder 0, then print. The only new part is the % 2 == 0 test.
A remainder of exactly 0 means even, so you compare with == 0.

exercises.prompt: Check. The code prints [4, 10, 2]. Your hand example was [4, 10, 2]. Verdict?
exercises.explanation: Output matches the by-hand list, so the even-filter is correct.

exercises.prompt: Same plan, new inputs: numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]. What prints?
exercises.explanation: 2 and 4 have remainder 0, so [2, 4]. The same filter handles new inputs.

exercises.prompt: To keep the ODD numbers instead, what single change would you make?
exercises.explanation: Only the condition changes: remainder 1 means odd. The empty-list + loop + append shape stays exactly the same.
